# Ocean Floor Report
Deep-sea exploration requires specialized titanium submersibles engineered to withstand crushing hydrostatic pressure across abyssal plains. Modern remotely operated vehicles carry high-definition optical cameras, robotic manipulator arms, and chemical mass spectrometers for sediment core sampling. Expedition vessels coordinate acoustic transponder beacons across wide survey grids during multi-week voyages in international waters. Marine geologists map basaltic ridges, fracture zones, and tectonic spreading centers along the mid-ocean mountain chains. Surface teams monitor telemetry streams continuously through fiber-optic tethers connected to shipboard control rooms. Calibration protocols ensure pressure sensors maintain sub-millimeter precision throughout extreme thermal shocks. Navigation sonar arrays avoid steep volcanic talus slopes during low-visibility descents into unexplored trenches. Standardised logging procedures archive video transects for global oceanographic repositories and open-access biodiversity atlases. Autonomous benthic landers remain anchored on the seabed for twelve months recording current velocities and dissolved oxygen levels. Long-term acoustic hydrophones capture low-frequency seismic tremors associated with subsea magma migration. Beyond geological mapping, biological surveys revealed that giant tube worms Riftia pachyptila lack a digestive tract and rely entirely on symbiotic sulfur-oxidizing bacteria for nutrition at 2,500 meters depth.
cases.script_paragraph: At 2,500 meters depth, giant tube worms have no digestive tract at all and depend completely on symbiotic sulfur-oxidizing bacteria to survive.
